skills.name: Equal Groups and Multiplication
skills.target: I can write a multiplication expression for a picture or story of equal groups and tell what each factor means.
skills.misconception: Mixing up the number of groups and the number in each group, or adding the two numbers (4 groups of 3 → 7).
skills.howToAddress: Have students circle each group, say “__ groups of __,” and check by skip counting the total.

skills.name: Arrays and Multiplication
skills.target: I can describe an array with rows and columns and find the total by multiplying.
skills.misconception: Counting the rows plus the columns, or counting only the dots along the edges.
skills.howToAddress: Cover all but one row: how many in one row? How many rows like it? Then multiply.

skills.name: Multiplying by 2, 5, and 10
skills.target: I can multiply by 2, 5, and 10 using skip counting and patterns.
skills.misconception: Losing count while skip counting, or adding a zero to products of 5 (5 × 7 = 70).
skills.howToAddress: Use a number line or hundred chart to skip count; connect 5s to half of 10s.

skills.name: Multiplication Word Problems
skills.target: I can solve equal-group, array, and measurement word problems by drawing a model and writing a multiplication equation.
skills.misconception: Adding the two numbers in the story because they both appear in it.
skills.howToAddress: Ask “Are there equal groups? How many groups? How many in each?” before choosing an operation.

skills.name: Division as Equal Sharing
skills.target: I can share a total equally among a number of groups and write a division equation for how many are in each group.
skills.misconception: Making groups that are not equal, or giving the number of groups as the answer.
skills.howToAddress: Deal out counters one at a time to each group; check that every group has the same number.

skills.name: Division as Equal Grouping
skills.target: I can make groups of a given size from a total and write a division equation for how many groups there are.
skills.misconception: Thinking every division asks “how many in each group,” so the answer names the wrong quantity.
skills.howToAddress: Label the answer with its meaning: “6 bags” or “6 in each bag.” Act out both kinds with the same numbers.

skills.name: Division as an Unknown Factor
skills.target: I can solve a division fact by finding the missing factor in a related multiplication fact and write fact families.
skills.misconception: Writing related facts in the wrong order (6 ÷ 42 = 7) or mixing up which number is the product.
skills.howToAddress: Use a triangle fact card: the product goes on top; cover a number and name the fact that finds it.

skills.name: Division Word Problems
skills.target: I can solve sharing and grouping word problems within 100 with a drawing and a division equation.
skills.misconception: Multiplying the two numbers in the story whenever the word “each” appears.
skills.howToAddress: Draw a tape diagram: is the total known? If the total is known and a group size or count is missing, divide.

skills.name: Commutative Property of Multiplication
skills.target: I can use the commutative property to turn an array or fact around and know the product stays the same.
skills.misconception: Believing the property works for division too (12 ÷ 3 = 3 ÷ 12).
skills.howToAddress: Rotate an array a quarter turn: rows become columns, the total does not change. Test a division example to see it fail.

skills.name: Associative Property of Multiplication
skills.target: I can regroup three factors to make multiplying easier and show the product is the same.
skills.misconception: Multiplying only two of the three factors, or adding one of them.
skills.howToAddress: Circle the two factors you will multiply first, write the partial product, then multiply by the third.

skills.name: Distributive Property: Break Apart Facts
skills.target: I can break a factor into two easier parts, multiply each part, and add the two products.
skills.misconception: Breaking apart one factor but multiplying only one part, or adding the leftover part instead of multiplying it.
skills.howToAddress: Draw the array and split it with a line; label each part with its own multiplication.

skills.name: Multiplying and Dividing with 0 and 1
skills.target: I can explain and use the rules for multiplying by 0 and 1 and dividing by 1 and by the same number.
skills.misconception: Thinking n × 0 = n, or that 0 ÷ n and n ÷ 0 behave the same.
skills.howToAddress: Tell equal-group stories: 5 plates with 0 cookies; 1 plate with 5 cookies. Explain why we cannot share into 0 groups.

skills.name: Fact Strategies for 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 9
skills.target: I can find any fact to 10 × 10 with a strategy such as doubling, adding a group, or subtracting a group.
skills.misconception: Making an off-by-one-group error (7 × 8 = 48) or using the strategy on the wrong fact.
skills.howToAddress: Name the known fact you start from and say how many groups you are adding or subtracting.

skills.name: Rounding to the Nearest 10
skills.target: I can round a whole number to the nearest 10 by finding the two tens it is between and deciding which is closer.
skills.misconception: Rounding down every time, or changing the hundreds digit when rounding to the nearest ten.
skills.howToAddress: Place the number on a number line between the two tens; a 5 in the ones place rounds up.

skills.name: Rounding to the Nearest 100
skills.target: I can round a whole number to the nearest 100 by finding the two hundreds it is between and deciding which is closer.
skills.misconception: Looking at the ones digit instead of the tens digit, or rounding 350 down.
skills.howToAddress: Underline the hundreds digit, look only at the tens digit, and check with a number line.

skills.name: Adding within 1,000
skills.target: I can add within 1,000 using place value strategies and the standard algorithm, regrouping when needed.
skills.misconception: Forgetting to regroup, or lining up digits by the left edge instead of by place.
skills.howToAddress: Use base‑ten blocks or a place-value chart; trade 10 ones for 1 ten and record the regrouped ten.

skills.name: Subtracting within 1,000
skills.target: I can subtract within 1,000 using place value strategies and the standard algorithm, including across zeros.
skills.misconception: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger digit in each place (“smaller from bigger”).
skills.howToAddress: Model with base‑ten blocks: when there are not enough ones, unbundle a ten. Check by adding.

skills.name: Estimating to Check Sums and Differences
skills.target: I can round to estimate a sum or difference and decide whether an exact answer is reasonable.
skills.misconception: Treating the estimate as the exact answer, or rounding each number to a different place.
skills.howToAddress: Estimate first, solve, then compare: is the exact answer close to the estimate?

skills.name: Unknown Numbers in Multiplication and Division Equations
skills.target: I can find the missing number in a multiplication or division equation in any position, such as 8 × ? = 48 or 5 = ? ÷ 3.
skills.misconception: Doing the operation shown on the two given numbers (for ? ÷ 3 = 5, answering 5 ÷ 3 or 15 ÷ 5).
skills.howToAddress: Read the equation as a sentence and test the answer by putting it back into the equation.

skills.name: Word Problems with Unknowns in Any Position
skills.target: I can write an equation with a symbol for the unknown when the total, the group size, or the number of groups is missing, and solve it.
skills.misconception: Writing the equation in the order the numbers appear instead of by their meaning.
skills.howToAddress: Sort the numbers into “groups,” “in each group,” and “total” before writing the equation.

skills.name: Multiplying by Multiples of 10
skills.target: I can multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 using place value, such as 4 × 60 = 4 × 6 tens = 24 tens = 240.
skills.misconception: Writing too many or too few zeros, or adding the zero to the wrong factor.
skills.howToAddress: Say the problem in tens: 4 × 6 tens = 24 tens. Then write 24 tens as 240.

skills.name: Patterns in the Addition and Multiplication Tables
skills.target: I can describe a pattern in an addition or multiplication table and explain it using properties or even and odd numbers.
skills.misconception: Describing a pattern without explaining why it happens, or over-generalizing (“all products are even”).
skills.howToAddress: Test the pattern with several examples and use equal groups to explain why (4 × n = 2 groups of 2 × n).

skills.name: Writing Equations for Two-Step Problems
skills.target: I can write an equation with a letter for the unknown to represent a two-step word problem.
skills.misconception: Writing an equation for only the first step, or using the letter for a number that is already known.
skills.howToAddress: Underline the question first; the letter stands for the answer to that question.

skills.name: Solving Two-Step Problems and Checking Reasonableness
skills.target: I can solve two-step word problems with the four operations and use rounding or mental math to check that the answer makes sense.
skills.misconception: Stopping after the first step, or not noticing that an answer is far from an estimate.
skills.howToAddress: Plan both steps with a tape diagram; estimate before solving and compare after.

skills.name: Unit Fractions and Equal Parts
skills.target: I can name the unit fraction 1/b for one of b equal parts of a whole and tell whether parts are equal.
skills.misconception: Naming a fraction for parts that are not equal, or writing the number of shaded parts over unshaded parts.
skills.howToAddress: Ask “Are all the parts the same size?” first; the denominator counts all the equal parts.

skills.name: Fractions Made from Unit Fractions
skills.target: I can explain that a/b is a copies of 1/b and name a fraction shown by a model or a story.
skills.misconception: Thinking a bigger denominator means bigger pieces, or counting unshaded parts as the numerator.
skills.howToAddress: Count unit fractions aloud: one‑fourth, two‑fourths, three‑fourths. The numerator counts how many parts.

skills.name: Unit Fractions on a Number Line
skills.target: I can partition the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal parts and locate 1/b on a number line.
skills.misconception: Counting the tick marks instead of the spaces, so thirds become fourths.
skills.howToAddress: Count the jumps (spaces) from 0 to 1, not the marks. Shade the first jump.

skills.name: Fractions on a Number Line
skills.target: I can locate a/b on a number line by marking off a lengths of 1/b from 0, including fractions greater than 1.
skills.misconception: Starting to count at the first tick mark instead of at 0, or relabeling past 1 as 1/b again.
skills.howToAddress: Make a jump for each unit fraction starting at 0 and count the jumps aloud; keep the same denominator past 1.

skills.name: Equivalent Fractions with Models
skills.target: I can use fraction bars and number lines to show that two fractions are equivalent because they are the same size or the same point.
skills.misconception: Comparing pictures of different-size wholes, or thinking fractions with different numbers can never be equal.
skills.howToAddress: Line up fraction strips of the same whole; equivalent fractions end at the same place.

skills.name: Generating Equivalent Fractions
skills.target: I can write a simple equivalent fraction (halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths) and explain why it is equivalent with a model.
skills.misconception: Adding the same number to the numerator and denominator (1/2 = 2/3).
skills.howToAddress: Split each part of a model into the same number of smaller parts and recount the parts.

skills.name: Whole Numbers as Fractions
skills.target: I can write a whole number as a fraction and recognize fractions such as 6/3 or 4/4 that equal whole numbers.
skills.misconception: Thinking 1 = 1/1 only, or that 3/1 means one‑third.
skills.howToAddress: Show 3 wholes each cut into 1 part (3/1) and 1 whole cut into 4 parts with all shaded (4/4).

skills.name: Comparing Fractions with the Same Denominator
skills.target: I can compare two fractions with the same denominator by comparing numerators, record with >, =, <, and justify with a model.
skills.misconception: Forgetting that the comparison only works when both fractions refer to the same whole.
skills.howToAddress: Use same-size fraction bars; same-size pieces means more pieces is more.

skills.name: Comparing Fractions with the Same Numerator
skills.target: I can compare two fractions with the same numerator by reasoning about the size of the pieces and justify with a model.
skills.misconception: Thinking the fraction with the larger denominator is larger (1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4).
skills.howToAddress: Share one sandwich among 4 people and among 8 people: who gets the bigger piece?

skills.name: Telling Time to the Nearest Minute
skills.target: I can read and write time to the nearest minute on an analog clock and a digital clock.
skills.misconception: Reading the hour hand as the next hour too early, or reading the minute hand’s number as minutes (on the 4 → 4 minutes).
skills.howToAddress: Count minutes by 5s around the clock, then by 1s; check that the hour hand is between two numbers.

skills.name: Elapsed Time
skills.target: I can find a start time, end time, or elapsed time in minutes using a number line or a clock.
skills.misconception: Treating an hour as 100 minutes, or subtracting times like whole numbers across the hour.
skills.howToAddress: Use an open number line: jump to the next hour, then jump the rest, and add the jumps.

skills.name: Measuring Liquid Volume in Liters
skills.target: I can read a liquid volume on a scaled container and estimate liquid volumes in liters.
skills.misconception: Reading each tick as 1 liter when the scale counts by 2s or 5s.
skills.howToAddress: Find the value of one tick first: count the spaces between two labeled marks.

skills.name: Measuring Mass in Grams and Kilograms
skills.target: I can read a mass on a scale, choose grams or kilograms, and estimate the mass of everyday objects.
skills.misconception: Choosing kilograms for light objects because the number would be smaller, or mixing up mass and size.
skills.howToAddress: Use benchmarks: a paper clip is about 1 gram; a large book is about 1 kilogram.

skills.name: Liquid Volume and Mass Word Problems
skills.target: I can add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems with masses or liquid volumes in the same units.
skills.misconception: Leaving off units or using the wrong operation for comparing amounts.
skills.howToAddress: Draw a beaker or tape diagram, label the units, and write an equation.

units.name: Graphs, Measurement Data, and Line Plots

skills.name: Reading Scaled Picture Graphs
skills.target: I can use the key of a scaled picture graph, including half symbols, to find and compare amounts.
skills.misconception: Counting each picture as 1 instead of using the key.
skills.howToAddress: Circle the key and skip count by its value for each row.

skills.name: Reading Scaled Bar Graphs
skills.target: I can read a scaled bar graph, including bars that end between grid lines, and solve one- and two-step how many more and how many less problems.
skills.misconception: Reading a bar that ends halfway between lines as the lower line, or adding when the question asks how many more.
skills.howToAddress: Trace the top of the bar to the scale; find the value halfway between two labels.

skills.name: Making Scaled Picture Graphs and Bar Graphs
skills.target: I can choose a scale and draw a scaled picture graph or bar graph that matches a data table.
skills.misconception: Using a scale that does not fit the data, or drawing a picture for every single item.
skills.howToAddress: Divide each number by the scale; use half symbols or bars that end between lines when needed.

skills.name: Measuring to the Nearest Half and Quarter Inch
skills.target: I can measure lengths to the nearest half inch and quarter inch with a ruler.
skills.misconception: Starting at 1 instead of 0, or counting tick marks instead of spaces.
skills.howToAddress: Line the object up at 0; find the whole inch, then count quarter-inch spaces past it.

skills.name: Making and Reading Line Plots
skills.target: I can make a line plot of measurement data marked in whole numbers, halves, or fourths and answer questions about it.
skills.misconception: Leaving out values with no data, or placing a mark at the wrong fraction.
skills.howToAddress: Label every tick on the scale first; cross off each data value as you plot it.

skills.name: Understanding Area and Unit Squares
skills.target: I can explain that area is the number of unit squares that cover a shape with no gaps or overlaps.
skills.misconception: Counting the squares around the edge, or accepting gaps and overlaps when tiling.
skills.howToAddress: Tile with real square tiles; check that there are no gaps or overlaps before counting.

skills.name: Measuring Area by Counting Unit Squares
skills.target: I can find area by counting unit squares and name it in square centimeters, square meters, square inches, square feet, or square units.
skills.misconception: Writing the unit as centimeters instead of square centimeters.
skills.howToAddress: Ask “What is one square worth?” and say the unit as “square ___.”

skills.name: Area of Rectangles: Tile and Multiply
skills.target: I can find the area of a rectangle by tiling and show that multiplying the side lengths gives the same area.
skills.misconception: Adding the side lengths (finding perimeter) when area is asked.
skills.howToAddress: Draw rows of unit squares: the number of rows times the squares in each row.

skills.name: Area and the Distributive Property
skills.target: I can split a rectangle with side lengths a and b + c into two rectangles and show that its area is a × b + a × c.
skills.misconception: Adding one side length instead of multiplying both parts by it.
skills.howToAddress: Cut the rectangle on grid paper and write the area of each part before adding.

skills.name: Area of Rectilinear Figures
skills.target: I can find the area of a rectilinear figure by splitting it into rectangles that do not overlap and adding their areas.
skills.misconception: Counting the overlap twice, or using a side length that belongs to the whole figure for one part.
skills.howToAddress: Shade each rectangle a different color and label its own side lengths before multiplying.

skills.name: Finding Perimeter
skills.target: I can find the perimeter of a polygon by adding all of its side lengths, including sides that are not labeled.
skills.misconception: Adding only the labeled sides of a rectangle, or counting the unit squares inside (area).
skills.howToAddress: Trace the outside with a finger and check off each side as you add it.

skills.name: Finding an Unknown Side Length
skills.target: I can find an unknown side length when I know the perimeter and the other side lengths.
skills.misconception: Subtracting only one side from the perimeter, or dividing the perimeter by the number of sides for a shape that is not regular.
skills.howToAddress: Add the known sides first, then subtract that sum from the perimeter; check by adding all sides.

skills.name: Same Perimeter or Same Area
skills.target: I can draw and compare rectangles that have the same perimeter and different areas, or the same area and different perimeters.
skills.misconception: Thinking that rectangles with the same perimeter must have the same area.
skills.howToAddress: List all the rectangles with a given perimeter in a table and find each area.

skills.name: Shape Attributes and Quadrilaterals
skills.target: I can sort shapes by their attributes and explain that rhombuses, rectangles, and squares are all quadrilaterals.
skills.misconception: Thinking a square is not a rectangle or a rhombus, or that every quadrilateral is one of these.
skills.howToAddress: Use an attribute checklist (4 sides, 4 right angles, 4 equal sides) and check every box for each shape.

skills.name: Partitioning Shapes into Equal Areas
skills.target: I can partition a shape into parts with equal area and name the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
skills.misconception: Thinking parts must be the same shape to have equal area, or naming unequal parts with a unit fraction.
skills.howToAddress: Count the unit squares in each part on grid paper to check that the areas are equal.
